{"id": "32:11/q15", "question": "What is reported about the Angel of Death's reach?", "turns_on": "Which narrated image describes his access to people at death.", "positions": [{"id": "32:11/q15/p1", "position": "The earth is set before him like a basin, tray, platter, bowl or palm, so he reaches any place.", "reasons": "Mujāhid's recurring comparison varies in vessel wording; al-Suddī likens souls to grain picked by a bird. Ibn ʿAbbās also transmits the bowl account. Qurṭubī notes an ungraded Prophetic narration; Ibn Kathīr calls Zuhayr b. Muḥammad's similar Prophetic transmission mursal."}, {"id": "32:11/q15/p2", "position": "His stride spans east to west.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās is cited by Thaʿlabī, Baghawī and Ṭabrisī; Ṭabrisī also joins it to the bowl report."}, {"id": "32:11/q15/p3", "position": "He spans the world, with four wings and a body between heaven and earth.", "reasons": "Muqātil and al-Kalbī add that his legs span the world and souls can be taken as though the world were in his palm; Kuran Yolu says colossal accounts with countless limbs, faces, eyes and tongues lack Qur'anic or sound-hadith basis and arose from Isrāʾīliyyāt."}, {"id": "32:11/q15/p4", "position": "He carries an east-to-west spear and strikes those whose appointed term ends.", "reasons": "Muʿādh b. Jabal's report says he examines people or faces twice daily and tells the dead they join the army of the dead."}, {"id": "32:11/q15/p5", "position": "He stands on a ladder between heaven and earth.", "reasons": "Baghawī's report says helpers draw the soul out and he takes it at the throat."}]}
{"id": "32:11/q16", "question": "What happened to the man sent to India after seeing the Angel of Death?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "32:11/q16/p1", "position": "Solomon sent him there by wind, fulfilling the angel's order to take his soul in India.", "reasons": "Khaythamah and Shahr b. Ḥawshab report that the man requested the journey after seeing the angel, who was surprised because his assigned place of death was India."}]}
{"id": "32:11/q17", "question": "What does the Anṣārī deathbed report say?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "32:11/q17/p1", "position": "The angel is gentle with believers, visits every household five times daily, and cannot take even a mosquito without God's order.", "reasons": "The Prophet asks the angel to treat a believing Anṣārī gently; Māwardī and Ibn Kathīr transmit through Jaʿfar, Qurṭubī and Ālūsī transmit parallel versions, and Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites the account. Jaʿfar connects the five visits to prayer times; Ibn Kathīr says for one who kept prayer the angel repels Satan and prompts testimony of faith. Ālūsī cites similar transmissions by al-Ṭabarānī, Abū Nuʿaym and Ibn Mandah."}]}
{"id": "32:11/q18", "question": "How often does the Angel of Death inspect homes?", "turns_on": "The reports give incompatible counts of daily visits.", "positions": [{"id": "32:11/q18/p1", "position": "Five times daily, at prayer times.", "reasons": "The Anṣārī narration and Jaʿfar's gloss make this frequency; Ibn Kathīr adds that the angel repels Satan and prompts faith for a prayer-keeping dying person."}, {"id": "32:11/q18/p2", "position": "Twice daily.", "reasons": "Mujāhid says he visits tents and masonry houses alike; Muʿādh's spear report likewise says he examines each face twice daily."}, {"id": "32:11/q18/p3", "position": "Seven times daily.", "reasons": "Kaʿb al-Aḥbār says he stands at each inhabited home's door to see if anyone's term has arrived."}]}
{"id": "32:11/q19", "question": "Why do illnesses appear before death?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "32:11/q19/p1", "position": "They warn of death and prevent people from blaming the Angel of Death.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī transmits the Prophet's account that illness and pain precede the final messenger, who neither wrongs the term nor the provision and will return until none remain. Qurṭubī reports the angel's complaint about being blamed and cursed and God's answer that illness would appear as the cause."}]}
{"id": "32:11/q20", "question": "What happens to the Angel of Death at the end?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "32:11/q20/p1", "position": "He dies after all creatures, when God orders him between Paradise and Hell.", "reasons": "Bursevī's report has him as the sole survivor; al-Ḍaḥḥāk's report says he first takes other angels' souls and then dies."}]}
{"id": "32:11/q21", "question": "Are spectacular descriptions of Azrāʾīl reliable?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "32:11/q21/p1", "position": "Colossal forms with innumerable limbs and faces, and a leaf naming the dead forty days ahead, lack Qur'anic or sound-hadith support.", "reasons": "Kuran Yolu traces the stories to Isrāʾīliyyāt spread by Jewish converts under Abū Bakr and ʿUmar; the reported four-wing and world-spanning descriptions are given by Muqātil and Thaʿlabī."}]}
{"id": "32:11/q22", "question": "What does وُكِّلَ بِكُمْ mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "32:11/q22/p1", "position": "He was entrusted as a deputy to carry out an assigned task for them.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī defines tawkīl as committing an affair to another; Bursevī adds reliance and deputation. Rāzī says the assignment means no neglect or delay at the appointed term."}]}
{"id": "32:11/q23", "question": "Why is the agent of وُكِّلَ left unstated?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "32:11/q23/p1", "position": "The passive foregrounds the ease and divine power behind commissioning the angel.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says the unstated commissioner is the Creator and the angel His servant."}]}
{"id": "32:11/q24", "question": "Does the angel's appointment support legal agency or compelled seizure of rights?", "turns_on": "Whether divine commissioning supplies a general legal analogy, or a narrower analogy for judicial seizure.", "positions": [{"id": "32:11/q24/p1", "position": "It supports the permissibility of appointing an agent.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī reports that some scholars infer agency from God's appointment of the Angel of Death."}, {"id": "32:11/q24/p2", "position": "It does not by itself establish ordinary legal agency.", "reasons": "Ibn al-ʿArabī says divine and human purposes differ; God's sending a Messenger or commanding alms likewise does not validate such analogies (7:158, 2:43)."}, {"id": "32:11/q24/p3", "position": "Read for its meaning, it supports a judge appointing someone to seize a due right by force.", "reasons": "Ibn al-ʿArabī says the seizure need not depend on the debtor's act or consent."}]}
{"id": "32:11/q25", "question": "What does returning to your Lord mean?", "turns_on": "Whether 'return' names resurrection and recompense or exclusive dependence on God.", "positions": [{"id": "32:11/q25/p1", "position": "Resurrection after death, followed by judgment and recompense from God.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Yaḥyā, Wāḥidī, Baghawī, Bayḍāwī, Nāṣafī, Abū Ḥayyān, Ibn Kathīr, Bursevī and Ālūsī give this sense. Rāzī says return requires renewed life; Ibn al-Jawzī names the Day of Recompense. Ṭabrisī says the return is called 'to God' to magnify reward and punishment. Biqāʿī says the Creator and nurturer gathers all and does not neglect wrongdoers. Ṭabāṭabāʾī identifies the earlier 'meeting' of 32:10 and notes that ثم delays return after death. Iṣlāḥī stresses that God alone, not supposed gods or intercessors, judges; he says post-sight confession is useless because intellect and moral awareness were the trial."}, {"id": "32:11/q25/p2", "position": "It can mean entering a state where only God can benefit or harm.", "reasons": "Māwardī reports this alongside the recompense interpretation."}]}
{"id": "32:11/q26", "question": "How is تُرْجَعُونَ read?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb is passive or active, changing the grammatical agent.", "positions": [{"id": "32:11/q26/p1", "position": "In the passive: 'you are returned.'", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān calls this the majority reading; Samīn calls it the common reading."}, {"id": "32:11/q26/p2", "position": "In the active: 'you return.'", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān, Samīn and Ālūsī attribute this to Zayd b. ʿAlī; Qirāʾāt ER notes the active Form I shifts agency to the subjects."}]}
{"id": "32:11/q27", "question": "What inward sense is given to death?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "32:11/q27/p1", "position": "It signifies repentance that kills the former self.", "reasons": "Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq cites 2:54, 'repent to your Maker and kill yourselves,' to explain the repentant as one who has killed himself. Bursevī quotes a Persian couplet urging washing off error before sudden seizure."}]}
{"id": "32:11/q28", "question": "What other angelic assignments are reported alongside the Angel of Death's?", "turns_on": "The reports describe different angels' assignments and priorities.", "positions": [{"id": "32:11/q28/p1", "position": "Gabriel, Michael and the Angel of Death hold distinct charges recorded until resurrection.", "reasons": "Ibn Sābiṭ says Gabriel handles scriptures, revelation, wartime victory and destructive events; Michael rain and plants; and the Angel of Death souls, with their records agreeing at resurrection."}, {"id": "32:11/q28/p2", "position": "Israfil accompanied the Prophet for three years before Gabriel's twenty years of Qur'anic revelation.", "reasons": "Al-Shaʿbī says Israfil taught words but no Qur'an; Ibn ʿAsākir says the Trumpet angel's assignment suits a mission heralding the Hour, and compares assignments to Dhū al-Qarnayn and Khālid b. Sinān."}, {"id": "32:11/q28/p3", "position": "Gabriel will be first to be reckoned because he was trustee over God's messengers.", "reasons": "ʿAṭāʾ b. al-Sāʾib gives this rationale."}]}

{"id": "32:12/q01", "question": "How does لو ترى frame the sight of the criminals?", "turns_on": "Whether لو is conditional or carries a wish, and whether a result must be supplied.", "positions": [{"id": "32:12/q01/p1", "position": "It is a conditional with an unspoken result.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari calls it counterfactual; al-Samin reports the dispute with al-Shaykh. Abu Hayyan's poem illustrates conditional لو with an expressed answer. Al-Samin notes an analysis that the answer is implied by context; al-Burhan says omitted answers to لو and لولا are common."}, {"id": "32:12/q01/p2", "position": "It expresses a wish that the Prophet could see his enemies humbled.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari makes this consolation for the harm they caused him. Al-Baydawi and al-Burhan also give the optative analysis. Abu Hayyan and Ibn Malik object that لو is not inherently optative and that even its wish use needs an answer; Ibn Malik supplies an omitted وددت. Al-Samin cites the poem about Kulayb; al-Alusi says its لو is conditional, while al-Khafaji allows a wish construction by usage."}, {"id": "32:12/q01/p3", "position": "Its condition and result are implicit in the surrounding wording.", "reasons": "Jishumi reports this further analysis."}]}
{"id": "32:12/q02", "question": "Who is addressed by ترى?", "turns_on": "Whether singular address singles out Muhammad, includes all viewers, or belongs to the earlier command to speak.", "positions": [{"id": "32:12/q02/p1", "position": "The address is general to anyone able to see.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj and Abu Ishaq take the singular Prophet address as including the community, citing 65:1. Al-Biqaʿi notes a possible shift from the criminals to the Prophet, but allows any observer. Al-Alusi says universal astonishment or the manifest nature of the scene motivates this usage; al-Itqan says its obviousness includes every viewer."}, {"id": "32:12/q02/p2", "position": "The Prophet is addressed specifically.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi take the view as consolation after deniers hurt him. Al-Biqaʿi says the shift signals contempt for them. Islahi says he would see helplessness beyond what he now imagines. Study Quran reports this address while noting the shared effect of amazement."}, {"id": "32:12/q02/p3", "position": "Muhammad is told to say the warning to a criminal.", "reasons": "Abu al-Abbas connects the sentence to the earlier قل and says its listener would regret past conduct; Abu Hayyan explains this link to يتوفاكم in 32:11."}]}
{"id": "32:12/q03", "question": "What result is left unsaid after 'if you saw'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "32:12/q03/p1", "position": "One would see an astonishing, dreadful sight and take the utmost lesson.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj implies a lesson; al-Thaʿlabi, al-Baghawi, al-Tabrisi, al-Burhan, al-Itqan and Bursawi supply wonder or dread. Al-Zamakhshari offers the worst imaginable state. Ibn ʿAtiyya and Jishumi say omission expands imagination and heightens terror. Al-Biqaʿi says the horror exceeds description; Islahi says the Prophet could not imagine the degree of helplessness now."}]}
{"id": "32:12/q04", "question": "What does ترى govern here?", "turns_on": "Whether seeing takes an object recovered from what follows.", "positions": [{"id": "32:12/q04/p1", "position": "It needs no expressed object and governs the time إذ.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi compares 76:20; al-Nasafi calls إذ an adverb of ترى. Al-Alusi prefers intransitive ترى because it fits astonishment of any viewer."}, {"id": "32:12/q04/p2", "position": "Its object is omitted or supplied by the following scene.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi supplies 'the criminals when they lower their heads'; al-Baydawi and al-Alusi supply the criminals or their bowing from what follows إذ."}]}
{"id": "32:12/q05", "question": "How is the opening clause parsed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "32:12/q05/p1", "position": "It forms a nominal construction with a supplied predicate.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas calls it a subject and predicate; al-Qurtubi says the predicate is supplied by the following construction."}]}
{"id": "32:12/q06", "question": "Why does إذ introduce a future scene?", "turns_on": "Whether إذ is figurative past usage for a certain future or replaces إذا.", "positions": [{"id": "32:12/q06/p1", "position": "The future event is expressed as past because its occurrence is certain.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi compares 6:27; al-Zamakhshari says what God guarantees is certain. Al-Samin says لو shifts the present into past and cites أتى أمر الله (16:1); al-Biqaʿi explains the imperfect after a past-associated particle as inviting anticipation. Al-Alusi grounds the past idiom in God's eternal knowledge."}, {"id": "32:12/q06/p2", "position": "إذ stands in place of إذا.", "reasons": "Abu al-Baqa proposes substitution; al-Samin says it is unnecessary given the other account."}]}
{"id": "32:12/q07", "question": "Who are المجرمون?", "turns_on": "Whether the definite noun picks up 32:10, denotes all criminals, or specifies a subgroup.", "positions": [{"id": "32:12/q07/p1", "position": "They are the deniers of resurrection mentioned earlier.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAtiyya cites the Hell threat and their later certainty; al-Nasafi and Bursawi identify those questioning recreation after dissolution in 32:10. Tabatabai appeals to the definite article and the verse's conclusion. Kuranyolu says context in 32:10–11 narrows the literal 'criminals/sinners' to unbelievers."}, {"id": "32:12/q07/p2", "position": "They are the polytheists or unbelievers.", "reasons": "Yahya, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir call them polytheists; Ibn ʿAtiyya says unbelievers because of the threat of Hell."}, {"id": "32:12/q07/p3", "position": "They are specifically the Meccan unbelievers.", "reasons": "Muqatil identifies them; al-Wahidi transmits him."}, {"id": "32:12/q07/p4", "position": "They are the whole class of criminals.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi gives the broader alternative to the previously mentioned deniers."}, {"id": "32:12/q07/p5", "position": "They are people who sever what God commanded to be joined.", "reasons": "Al-Biqaʿi gives this characterization."}]}
{"id": "32:12/q08", "question": "What does ناكسوا رؤوسهم describe?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "32:12/q08/p1", "position": "They lower their heads in shame, regret, grief, humiliation and distress.", "reasons": "Yahya, al-Tabari, al-Thaʿlabi, al-Mawardi's transmitters, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, Ibn ʿAtiyya, al-Tabrisi, al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Kathir, al-Biqaʿi, Bursawi and al-Alusi give these shades. Al-Wahidi says a regretful person looks down in confused thought; al-Razi compares a servant facing the lord he wronged. Tabatabai gives the physical sense. Jishumi, al-Tabrisi and Bursawi explain naks as turning upside down; illness relapse has ḍamma, a reversed arrow kasra."}]}
{"id": "32:12/q09", "question": "How does ناكسوا رؤوسهم work as a participial construction?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "32:12/q09/p1", "position": "The ongoing active participle loses its plural nun in annexation to its object without becoming definite.", "reasons": "Sibawayh says an ongoing participle governs like a present verb; loss of tanwin or plural nun eases pronunciation, putting the object in genitive. He cites this verse, other Qur'anic constructions (3:185, 54:27, 5:1–2, 5:95, 46:24), and poets including Zuhayr, al-Farazdaq, al-Zibriqan, al-Sulayk, al-Nabigha and al-Marrar. Al-Khalil's هو كائن أخيك illustrates the light form. Sibawayh distinguishes completed action and discusses genitive or accusative coordination, elision, long separation (6:96), and two-object order (14:47); Isa's Abu al-Aswad variant is poetic necessity. Al-Wahidi compares ثاني عطفه (22:9) and هديا بالغ الكعبة (5:95), referring to 4:97."}]}
{"id": "32:12/q10", "question": "How is the head-bowing phrase read?", "turns_on": "Whether the first word is a participle or past verb.", "positions": [{"id": "32:12/q10/p1", "position": "The common reading has an active participle annexed to its object.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and al-Samin contrast it with Zayd's verb reading."}, {"id": "32:12/q10/p2", "position": "Zayd ibn Ali reads نكسوا رؤوسهم as a past verb and direct object.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and al-Samin transmit it."}]}

{"id": "32:12/q12", "question": "How is their cry 'رَبَّنَا' introduced grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether to supply a verb of saying, construe the utterance directly as a circumstance, or supply an appeal.", "positions": [{"id": "32:12/q12/p1", "position": "An unspoken 'they say' introduces their words.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, al-Zajjaj, Ibn ʿAtiyya, al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi and al-Burhan supply a speech verb. Al-Razi says its omission signals shame too intense for speech. Al-Samin calls the utterance circumstantial and says omitted قول is more usual than al-Zamakhshari's proposed appeal."}, {"id": "32:12/q12/p2", "position": "The quoted plea itself is a circumstantial utterance governed by ناكسوا.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi prefers this account over supplying يستغيثون بقولهم."}, {"id": "32:12/q12/p3", "position": "An unspoken 'they appeal for help by saying' introduces it.", "reasons": "Al-Samin attributes this to al-Zamakhshari and prefers the more common ellipsis of قول; al-Alusi contrasts it with his preferred circumstantial analysis."}]}
{"id": "32:12/q13", "question": "What do they mean by 'we have seen and heard'?", "turns_on": "What the objects of sight and hearing are, and whether the admission concerns worldly perception or the witnessed afterlife.", "positions": [{"id": "32:12/q13/p1", "position": "They now see the truth they denied and hear the messengers' truth or words.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari specifies punishment and the messengers; Ibn Isa says God's warning and their confirmation. Al-Wahidi says they see what they ignored and hear what they denied. The declaration comes too late to help, as Yahya, Qatada, al-Qurtubi and al-Durr stress. Al-Alusi describes seeing resurrection and hearing the messengers obediently; Ibn Kathir cites 19:38."}, {"id": "32:12/q13/p2", "position": "They see God's promise or threat fulfilled and hear God confirm His messengers.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari, al-Tabrisi, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi give this pairing; al-Biqaʿi adds hearing God, angels and Fire. Al-Alusi instead specifies God's question to humans and jinn about messengers (6:130)."}, {"id": "32:12/q13/p3", "position": "They see their sins and hear what is said about them.", "reasons": "Qatada says this comes when perception cannot benefit them. Al-Alusi gives a variant: they see the ugliness of deeds once thought good and hear angels say they return to the Fire."}, {"id": "32:12/q13/p4", "position": "They were like blind and deaf people, but now truly see and hear.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari, al-Tabrisi, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Bursawi and al-Alusi describe newly effective faculties or recognition of visible and audible signs; al-Irshad adds their claim that sound hearts can now understand and act. Al-Qurtubi says they perceived in life but failed to reflect."}, {"id": "32:12/q13/p5", "position": "They confess that they had seen messengers and heard them in worldly life.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi says they also saw God's marvels, leaving no excuse; Abu Hayyan repeats this reading. Al-Alusi reports the messengers version."}, {"id": "32:12/q13/p6", "position": "They confess to seeing creative signs and hearing revealed signs in worldly life.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports the proof-against-them reading and calls it weak."}, {"id": "32:12/q13/p7", "position": "They see guidance and hear truth.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi gives this broad explanation; Tabatabai distinguishes direct vision from obedient hearing."}, {"id": "32:12/q13/p8", "position": "They now hear God's words and obey His command.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir compares 19:38; Tabatabai also calls their hearing obedient."}]}
{"id": "32:12/q14", "question": "Do أبصرنا and سمعنا require expressed objects?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "32:12/q14/p1", "position": "Their objects are omitted, or the verbs mean that they became seeing and hearing.", "reasons": "Al-Samin offers both analyses."}]}
{"id": "32:12/q15", "question": "Why is sight mentioned before hearing?", "turns_on": "Whether the order foregrounds direct visual certainty or connects hearing to the promised action.", "positions": [{"id": "32:12/q15/p1", "position": "They heard of resurrection in life but now see it directly and gain certainty.", "reasons": "Al-Samarrai says hearing ordinarily leads because it is vital for instruction, has shorter range and develops earlier; a blind listener can be taught, while deafness impedes instruction. Here direct vision settles what they had heard and doubted. Ubayy's lists add the smoke, violent seizure or assault, al-lizām/al-luzūm and, in some transmissions, the Romans; the reports vary over whether seizure or smoke is named, and Ibn Kathīr says one version makes the assault and al-lizām still future while calamities and smoke had passed. Muslim preserves Shuʿba's uncertainty between assault and smoke. The Prophet's reported list gives misfortunes, illnesses and burdens/anṣāb: chastening for the profligate, purification or expiation for believers. Ibn Kathīr reports al-Suddī's detail that every Meccan household lost or ransomed a relative. The Study Quran adds defeat, humiliation and natural disaster. Al-Zamakhsharī reports the same explanation through al-Ālūsī."}, {"id": "32:21/q11/p3", "position": "Later people refrain from the earlier sinners' acts.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī reports this as an alternative to the sinners' own repentance."}, {"id": "32:21/q11/p4", "position": "An inward return to sincere seeking and love after heedlessness.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says hardship cleanses primordial nature before corruption and veiling. {"id": "32:21/q12", "question": "Who can return if the punishment kills some of them?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "32:21/q12/p1", "position": "Those who survive or remain may repent; the pronouns can refer to different subsets.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā b. Sallām applies the phrase to those left alive. Ibn ʿAṭiyya makes the differing pronoun references explicit on the sword interpretation. Al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, Ibn Masʿūd and Bursawī agree; al-Biqāʿī says some first turned from fear of the sword and later loved Islam after seeing its merits."}]}
{"id": "32:21/q13", "question": "How can God express hope for their return while knowing the outcome?", "turns_on": "How divine knowledge, divine will, servants' choice and the conventional use of hope language relate.", "positions": [{"id": "32:21/q13/p1", "position": "Hope language describes an act whose outcome is not entailed by that act, even if independently known.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī compares a trader hoping for profit despite independent certainty with cutting a throat 'hoping' for death, which is impossible because death follows from the act itself. Punishment does not itself guarantee repentance. He also offers that God chastens gradually like one who hopes, or that observers might say 'perhaps they return'; 26:82 and 29:36 show hope language beside certainty, while 32:14 is noted in the discussion."}, {"id": "32:21/q13/p2", "position": "God wills servants' free return even if He knows they will refuse; this does not imply inability.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī says the hoped-for return proves God wills everyone's return, against the Mujbira. Al-Zamakhsharī distinguishes God's own acts, which necessarily happen when He wills them, from His willing servants to choose obedience, and compares a person wishing a servant would obey. Al-Ālūsī reports and dismisses al-Zamakhsharī's interpretation of divine hope as willing; Abū Ḥayyān rejects the account as Muʿtazilī doctrine, saying Sunnis refuted it."}]}
{"id": "32:21/q14", "question": "What does the transmitted report about Ubayy's statement establish?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "32:21/q14/p1", "position": "Ubayy is reported to include named worldly events, though the wording and chain vary.", "reasons": "The Musnad report says calamities and smoke had passed and names al-baṭsha and al-lizām. Al-Ṭabarī notes variants over seizure versus smoke. Ibn Kathīr says Muslim has a similar stopped report and al-Bukhārī a report from Ibn Masʿūd; another wording separates past smoke from future assault and lizām. Muslim preserves Shuʿba's uncertainty between assault and smoke. Abū Mūsā notes that Yaḥyā b. Saʿīd's first transmission omits Yaḥyā b. al-Jazzār, one link in Ubayy's chain."}]}
{"id": "32:21/q15", "question": "What occasion of revelation is reported for these verses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "32:21/q15/p1", "position": "A report links them to al-Walīd ibn ʿUqba vying with ʿAlī at Badr.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī transmits this report without further evaluation in the note."}]}
{"id": "32:21/q16", "question": "How does the verse fit the sūra's progression?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "32:21/q16/p1", "position": "It sets the opponents' worldly warning and final fate beside the believers' worship and hidden reward.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says believers bow to the Qur'anic signs, pray at night and spend for God, with a concealed reward; the succeeding material contrasts their fate with opponents' worldly and next-world fate. The Study Quran describes the sūra's second half as contrasting prostration before signs with turning away, then recalling Israel's guidance through those signs, citing 32:15–22. Al-Biqāʿī says the promise answers believers' haste for opponents' worldly humiliation and counters opponents' denial of punishment after death and confidence in their numbers and strength. Kur'an Yolu says 32:22 confirms that stubbornness after opportunities to return deserves punishment."}]}
{"id": "32:21/q17", "question": "What is the revelation setting of the sūra containing this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "32:21/q17/p1", "position": "Sūrat al-Sajdah is Makkan.", "reasons": "The Study Quran identifies the sūra as Makkan; al-Biqāʿī places Quraysh's later drought, division and losses after its Meccan revelation."}]}
{"id": "33:5/q01", "question": "How should adoptees be named?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "33:5/q01/p1", "position": "By their biological fathers rather than their adopters.", "reasons": "Muqatil and Tabari name Zayd son of Haritha; Ibn Abbas says the men who begot them; Tabarsi allows the father of the marital bed. Elmalili and Asad emphasize true identity and public welfare. Alusi notes the wording covers girls too. Qurtubi defines an adopted claimant as one called another man's son and notes daʿwa with kasra; unknown lineage means patronage and religious brotherhood."}]}
{"id": "33:5/q02", "question": "What does the lām before 'fathers' convey?", "turns_on": "Naming usage, descent, or specification.", "positions": [{"id": "33:5/q02/p1", "position": "It follows Arabic usage for being called after someone.", "reasons": "Akhfash cites huwa yudʿā li-fulān."}, {"id": "33:5/q02/p2", "position": "It marks descent or affiliation.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur adduces poetry and the report of Umama daughter of Zaynab and Abu al-As; 'daughter of' can be implicit."}, {"id": "33:5/q02/p3", "position": "It specifies the fathers as those to whom they are attributed.", "reasons": "Tabatabai states this reading."}]}
